note:
v1, THE SKELETON of the album's fourth song: RUNNING TOTAL. Harry, 15 Nov about 02:42: "we can do fourth track same climber". The tooling's draw was Odd Sympathy (the new slot stood at 97% and the draw fell on the other 3%); I took his word and skeletoned the new song, as with songs two and three.
THE IDEA: one riff, two bars long, that is never simply played: it is ADDED UP. First its first note; then its first two; then its first three; each time from the top and one place further. Against a kit that keeps four in a bar, the riff's first note lands somewhere new every time. The sums work out exactly: the first statement to begin on a bar line again is the first WHOLE riff, a minute in. Then the same sum from the other end (its last note, its last two ...), and at the end the sum undone, the riff losing its first note each time until one is left.
ITS OWN COLOUR: a marimba (wood: an abacus) counts where the band does not: the first eight statements, the middle, the last eight.
THE SHAPE (4:31): 0:00 the marimba counts; 0:05 one guitar, bass and kick; 0:18 two guitars; 0:39 four; 1:04 the riff whole, on the bar line; 1:08 the whole riff eight times (up to A flat at 1:25); 1:41 the sum from the other end, on the marimba (bass and kick 1:59, the band 2:20); 2:50 the whole riff on C, home on F at 3:06; 3:23 the sum undone; 4:22 the marimba counts down alone; 4:27 one chord.

WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen): compscore 89.20 / 90.72 (seeds 0 and 11). File -10.0 LUFS, true peak -1.29. On the groove its full sections sit where the other three songs' do (-16.5 to -16.8 LUFS raw); the marimba alone is 6 to 8 dB quieter.
- Without the marimba the scorer heard one texture for four and a half minutes (64); with it, five or six sections (89 to 91). It still wants more difference between sections.
WHAT IT IS NOT YET: a skeleton. No voice, no lead, one rig, one riff; the kit only keeps time.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a riff that grows by a note is a hook or an exercise; whether the first minute, before the riff is whole, holds.
NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.
next: the riff itself (its hook, its rests); a kit that does more than keep time; a second rig; what the middle wants; read it against the records

note:
v2, THE TOTAL HAS A TUNE (1:25-1:41). The tooling drew this song and a section round; its map named the stretch where the riff, whole at last, was simply played eight times.
The riff has nine notes that are not the low string: the album's hook. In the riff they go by in a sixteenth or two. Now, when the whole riff moves up to A flat at 1:25, a lead guitar plays only those nine, each held until the next, each starting exactly where the riff hits it. It is the tune that was inside the riff all along, drawn out over the band.

note:
v3, THE SECOND COUNT IS SAID QUIETLY, AND THE BASS FOLLOWS THE KEY (whole song). The tooling drew this song and a section round; I took a whole-song round, because both things this song was owed are whole-song matters, and say so.
1. THE SECOND COUNT (1:41-2:50). The riff is added up twice, and both times the band came in a third of the way through and stayed: full band from 0:39 to the end. Now the second sum is the song's quiet middle, and it grows like a sum. The marimba counts alone; a clean guitar joins it (1:46); a second clean guitar on the other side (1:59); the bass and kick come back softly (2:20); and the band comes in for the last four statements (2:33, on a crash). The low end is gone for forty seconds. Two clean guitars are new to this song.
2. THE BASS FOLLOWS THE KEY. The fault found on Plain Hunt: the bass's tone controls were set for the low F, and on A flat, B and C its body was pushed down. They now follow the key.

note:
v4, THE TUNE IS ADDED UP TOO (section round, the second total, 2:50-3:23, as drawn). The map called it static: the whole riff eight times, as the first total was, and without the first total's tune.
The riff was a sum; now its tune is one. Over the second total the lead plays the riff's hook notes as the riff strikes them: only the first two in the first statement, holding the second; then three; one more each time. There are eight statements and the tune has nine notes, so the tune is whole exactly once: in the last statement, at home on F, just as the melt begins to take the riff apart. On C it sits an octave under, so it rises as it comes home. And the kit shapes the stretch: half time on C while the tune is short, the backbeat when the key comes home.

note:
v5, THE CHINA COUNTS (whole song, as drawn). The song's one idea is a sum: each statement starts again and goes one place further. But the kit only kept time: the china rode the beat through the build exactly as it does when the riff is whole. Now, wherever the riff is being added up or taken apart, the china strikes where each statement STARTS, with the kick and the open string, and a hat keeps the time. Its strokes come further apart as the statements grow (from 0:17) and closer together as the riff melts (3:23 to the end). When the riff is whole (the two totals) the china rides the bar as before: the cymbal alone tells you whether the riff is being counted or is complete.

note:
v6, THE RIFF WHOLE HAS ITS OWN RIG (palette round, as drawn). All four guitars were one rig, the album's most used, and the same four played the riff being counted and the riff complete. Now, in the two totals and on the last chord, the second pair is another rig: Common Time's wall (a darker, thicker amp and cabinet), in the form whose rests stay rests. Wherever the riff is being counted the tight pair plays as before. So the guitars now say what the china says: counted, the riff is tight; whole, it is a wall.

note: CORRECTION to v6's note (chirper-zero, 23:10): the six points are NOT the scorer finding a section where the riff becomes whole. I wrote that before I had looked. secsim shows the one section it added, at every cut, is the last four seconds: the final chord, which now has the wall rig on it, is cut off as a section of its own, and a four-second section holding one chord swings the scorer's density figure (0.08 to 0.45). Where the riff becomes whole (1:06) is a seam for the scorer in neither v5 nor v6. So the score says nothing about this swap either way; the measurements of the guitars stand; whether it is bigger or muddier is the card rt-wall.

v7, THE TUNE MELTS TOO (section round, 3:18-3:51, as drawn: the melt's first half minute, which the map called static and "little new" against the total before it).
The riff was added up, and so was its tune (the lead, over the second total). The riff is taken apart in the melt; now so is the tune. Through the melt the lead goes on playing the riff's hook notes where the riff strikes them, and as the riff loses its front the tune loses its first note: nine notes for four statements, eight from 3:38 (the A flat has gone), seven from 3:48 (the B), six from 4:00, five at 4:07. A thirty-two-place riff losing one chug is hard to hear; a nine-note tune losing its first note is not: the melt can now be followed by ear. The lead stops where the second pair of guitars does (4:09), and the marimba, which comes in there, carries what is left of the tune down to its last note. The lead sinks as it goes (5 dB by its end).
The line runs past the window, to 4:09: it stops where the band thins, not where the map's window ends.
